case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ADA “tester” who visits a hotel’s online reservation system solely to check for required accessibility information—without any intent to book a room—suffers a concrete injury sufficient for Article III standing when the information is allegedly missing.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing / case-or-controversy requirement), and Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189 (especially 42 U.S.C. § 12182 and the Attorney General’s implementing regulations, including the ADA hotel reservation accessibility-information rule, 28 C.F.R. Part 36).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Acheson Hotels argues Laufer lacks Article III standing because she had no concrete, real-world injury: she never intended to book a room at the hotel and sought the information only to generate litigation. In Acheson’s view, a bare regulatory noncompliance or an abstract desire to see information posted online is not enough; informational-injury standing requires downstream, practical consequences, and extending standing here would improperly expand ‘tester’ standing beyond its proper bounds and unsettle Article III limits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Laufer argues she has standing because the ADA and its reservation regulations create a right for disabled individuals to receive specific accessibility information on hotel booking channels, and denial of that information is itself a concrete discriminatory injury (an informational injury) regardless of her motive or intent to use the hotel. She relies on the principle that ‘tester’ status does not defeat standing when the plaintiff is denied information or treated differently in a manner the statute prohibits.
key_precedents: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190 (2021)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
United States v. Symonevich, 688 F.3d 12 (1st Cir. 2012)
In re Sealed Case, 151 F.3d 1059 (D.C. Cir. 1998)
McCoy v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 950 F.2d 13 (1st Cir. 1991)
United States v. Báez-Martínez, 950 F.3d 119 (1st Cir. 2020)
Bais Yaakov of Spring Valley v. ACT, Inc., 798 F.3d 46 (1st Cir. 2015)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—drawing on Havens Realty—is that the denial of accessibility information is itself unequal treatment and thus a concrete dignitary injury even for a tester. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Spokeo and TransUnion require more than the existence of a regulatory entitlement; the asserted harm must be concrete in the Article III sense, with a real-world nexus to the plaintiff’s conduct or a close historical analogue, and Laufer’s self-initiated review of a public website with no intent to book looks like an abstract interest in enforcement. Havens is meaningfully narrower because it involved a direct, transaction-like encounter and an individualized misrepresentation directed at the plaintiff—closer to historically cognizable fraud/dignitary injury—whereas an omission on a generally available webpage, untethered to any sought benefit, risks converting federal courts into roving compliance monitors (Justice Gorsuch’s concern). A minimalist disposition on standing preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves room for suits by would-be bookers or DOJ enforcement without deciding the regulation’s validity here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the denial of accessibility information is itself a concrete discriminatory injury, akin to the tester injury in Havens Realty. But Havens involved a personalized, unlawful misrepresentation directed to the plaintiff in a transaction-like exchange, which closely resembles historically cognizable fraud and dignitary harms; here, Laufer encountered only a generalized omission on a public webpage with no intent to book and no denial of any benefit she sought. Under TransUnion and Spokeo—as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—an asserted informational injury without adverse effects or practical nexus to the plaintiff’s conduct is not a concrete injury in fact, and treating a self-initiated compliance check as injury would expand Article III beyond its original public meaning. Whatever Congress or DOJ may have sought to accomplish through Title III regulations, they cannot constitutionally convert federal courts into roving enforcers absent a concrete, personal stake in the dispute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the ADA/DOJ reservation rule makes the withholding of accessibility information the unequal treatment itself, and that Havens allows tester standing for such a denial. But Havens involved a direct, individualized misrepresentation in a transaction-like interaction, which supplies a close historical analogue (fraud/dignitary harm) and a personal, concrete encounter; here, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, Laufer alleges only a generalized omission on a public website with no intent to use the information, which Spokeo and TransUnion treat as an “injury in law” lacking concreteness absent some real-world nexus. Accepting respondent’s theory would, as Justice Kavanaugh warns, let any self-appointed auditor manufacture standing by browsing for regulatory noncompliance, effectively converting Article III courts into compliance monitors—an institutional consequence the Constitution does not permit. The better course is a narrow standing holding that preserves suits by would-be bookers (or cases with actual impediment to use) and leaves broader enforcement to DOJ or plaintiffs with a concrete stake.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s TransUnion/Spokeo point seriously: Article III does not permit Congress or an agency to transform every regulatory omission into a concrete injury. But this case is not a free-floating “informational injury” asserted by any member of the public; as Justice Kagan emphasizes, Laufer alleges she personally encountered an ADA-governed reservation interface that withheld accessibility information that DOJ has made part of equal access, inflicting immediate unequal-treatment and dignitary harm akin to Havens’s tester injury. Justice Kavanaugh’s “no intent to book” requirement improperly adds a downstream-consequence prerequisite that would, in practical effect, force disabled individuals to assume the burdens and risks of travel planning before they can challenge threshold barriers designed to exclude them. Justice Gorsuch’s “roving compliance tribunal” concern is better handled through limits on traceability/redressability and on the scope of injunctive relief, rather than by adopting a standing rule that would insulate a common form of online discrimination from private enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that TransUnion and Spokeo caution against treating a bare “informational injury” as enough, especially where the plaintiff looks like a self-appointed compliance monitor. But that characterization fits best when the statute creates only a procedural reporting duty divorced from the plaintiff’s legally protected participation; here, Title III’s text guaranteeing “full and equal enjoyment,” together with the reservation-rule’s integration of accessibility information into equal access, makes the omission itself a discriminatory barrier encountered by this plaintiff—closer to Havens’s denial of information on unequal terms than to TransUnion’s no-real-world-impact category. Justice Barrett’s insistence on a downstream transactional consequence adds a requirement those cases do not impose when the harm alleged is the experienced deprivation of information the law makes integral to equal access, and tester motive does not negate that encounter under Havens. Justice Gorsuch’s “roving compliance tribunal” concern is real, but it is better managed through narrow construction of what the regulation demands and through traceability/redressability and injunctive-relief limits, rather than by redefining concreteness to exclude a core civil-rights informational denial.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest case that the ADA/DOJ reservation rule renders the denial of accessibility information itself unequal treatment, analogizing to Havens’s tester standing. But Havens turned on a direct, individualized misrepresentation in a transaction-like encounter—an inherently personal injury with a close common-law analogue—while this case involves a generalized omission on a public website coupled with no intent to use the information, which under Spokeo and TransUnion looks like an injury in law untethered to any concrete stake. Accepting the respondent’s theory risks allowing executive-branch rulemaking to define Article III injury and would invite the “roving compliance tribunal” problem the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett identify, eroding separation-of-powers limits. A narrow standing disposition leaves room for suits by would-be bookers and for public enforcement while preserving the Constitution’s requirement of a concrete, plaintiff-specific injury.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest case that DOJ’s reservation rule renders the missing accessibility information itself an unequal-treatment harm, analogizing to Havens and stressing dignitary injury even absent intent to book. But TransUnion and Spokeo (as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize) require more than a legislatively or regulatorily conferred entitlement; the plaintiff must show a concrete injury with a close historical analogue and some real-world nexus to her own conduct, and a self-initiated scan of a public webpage with no plan to transact looks like an abstract interest in enforcement. Havens is meaningfully narrower because it involved a direct, transaction-like interaction and an individualized misrepresentation to the plaintiff—features that map onto historically cognizable fraud/dignitary harms—whereas a generalized omission on a publicly available website lacks that personal, relational component. A narrow standing disposition preserves Article III limits without foreclosing suits by would-be bookers who are actually hindered in making a reservation or otherwise using the service.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the DOJ reservation rule makes the informational deficit itself the unequal treatment, bringing this within Havens even for a tester. But under Spokeo and especially TransUnion—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize—Article III requires a concrete injury with a close historical analogue, and Laufer’s self-initiated review of a generally available webpage with no intent to book or otherwise use the information looks like an abstract interest in compliance rather than a personal deprivation tied to real-world conduct. Havens, as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch stress, involved a direct, individualized misrepresentation in a transaction-like exchange, mapping onto historically cognizable fraud/dignitary harms; a passive omission on a public website lacks that personalized interaction and any reliance or downstream consequence for this plaintiff. I would therefore resolve narrowly on standing, while leaving open suits by plaintiffs who actually seek to reserve lodging and are concretely hindered by missing accessibility information.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that TransUnion’s “no adverse effects” language bars standing where a plaintiff has no downstream reliance—assumes the only cognizable harm is economic or transactional consequence, but Title III’s equal-access framework and DOJ’s reservation rule make the withheld accessibility information part of the discriminatory barrier itself. Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch’s “roving compliance monitor” concern is real, yet it overreads Spokeo/TransUnion as categorically excluding concrete dignitary/exclusionary injuries that occur at the threshold of participation, and it underweights Havens’s core principle that being personally subjected to unequal informational treatment is an injury even when the plaintiff is a tester. Havens is not limited to affirmative lies or face-to-face interactions; the salient analogue is discriminatory denial of information the law requires to be available on equal terms, which is historically tied to exclusion and humiliation harms, not mere “injury in law.” On pragmatic grounds consistent with my methodology, adopting Petitioners’ view would effectively insulate a significant category of online ADA access barriers from private enforcement, forcing disabled individuals to risk unusable travel or forgo the market—an unacceptable practical consequence for a statute structured to prevent exclusion at the outset.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, and this Court has made clear that “an asserted informational injury that causes no adverse effects cannot satisfy Article III.” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190, 2214 (2021); see also Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016). Unlike Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)—where the tester was personally subjected to a statutorily prohibited misrepresentation in a direct transactional interaction—Laufer alleges only the absence of regulatory disclosures on a website while conceding she had no intent to book, and thus no downstream use or denial of access to accommodation under 42 U.S.C. § 12182. A narrow ruling dismissing for lack of standing avoids expanding federal jurisdiction to police bare regulatory noncompliance, preserves institutional limits, and leaves enforcement primarily to the political branches (including DOJ) and to plaintiffs who seek to use the service and are concretely harmed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III limits the judicial power to concrete cases and controversies, and a plaintiff who visits a hotel’s reservation website with no intent to book a room alleges no real-world, personal stake beyond a claimed regulatory defect. Under Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, a bare statutory or regulatory violation—without concrete harm closely related to a traditionally cognizable injury—does not suffice, and an asserted “informational injury” requires more than an abstract interest in compliance. Havens Realty is distinguishable because the tester there was personally subjected to discriminatory misrepresentation in a transaction-like interaction, whereas here the plaintiff received the same publicly available (allegedly incomplete) information as any user and suffered no denial of a benefit she sought. Construing Title III and the Attorney General’s regulations to confer standing on any self-appointed “tester” with no intent to use the accommodation would improperly expand federal judicial power beyond the Constitution’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete injury, and a bare failure to provide information required by regulation—without any intent to book a room or otherwise use the service—resembles the kind of purely statutory violation that Spokeo and TransUnion held insufficient. Title III of the ADA, 42 U.S.C. § 12182, targets discrimination in the "full and equal enjoyment" of public accommodations, and Laufer’s self-inflicted visit to a reservation webpage solely to generate litigation does not plausibly impair her enjoyment of any offered service in a real-world way. Havens Realty is distinguishable because it involved an individualized, discriminatory misrepresentation made “because of race” to the tester herself, whereas this case alleges an abstract informational deficit unconnected to any planned transaction or downstream consequence. Allowing standing on these facts would expand federal jurisdiction to policing regulatory compliance at the behest of uninjured private attorneys general, with serious practical consequences for Article III limits and regulated entities.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III and the Attorney General’s reservation regulations create a right for disabled users to receive specified accessibility information through hotel booking channels, and the denial of that information is a concrete discriminatory injury akin to the “tester” injury recognized in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363, 373–74 (1982). Under Spokeo and TransUnion, a statutory violation alone is not enough, but where the statute protects against unequal treatment and the plaintiff personally experiences that denial in the transaction interface, the harm bears a close relationship to historically cognizable dignitary/discriminatory injuries and is not merely abstract. Laufer’s lack of intent to book does not negate injury because Article III does not require a plaintiff to intend to consummate a transaction to be injured by being denied information on unequal terms; “tester” status does not defeat standing where the statute makes the denial itself unlawful. Denying standing here would undercut Congress’s chosen enforcement scheme for widespread, hard-to-police access barriers that disproportionately burden people with disabilities, for whom timely, reliable accessibility information is often essential to equal participation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III and the Attorney General’s reservation-accessibility regulation create a legally protected right for disabled users to receive specified accessibility information through hotel reservation systems, and the alleged denial of that information is an injury of the type the statute targets. Under Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, a tester’s lack of intent to rent (or here, to book) does not defeat standing where the plaintiff is personally denied information or truthful treatment the statute requires. Spokeo and TransUnion do not foreclose standing because this is not a bare procedural violation divorced from the plaintiff; it is the concrete withholding of statutorily required information from a member of the protected class, akin to the informational injury recognized in Havens and later informational-injury cases. Workability and coherence favor treating the regulatory right to accessibility information as enforceable by those the ADA protects, while leaving merits and remedial limits to the statutory scheme (not Article III).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, and a plaintiff cannot establish standing by pointing to a bare regulatory violation divorced from any real-world harm. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez and Spokeo, a statutory “informational” right is not enough where the plaintiff neither sought to use the information for any practical purpose nor suffered downstream consequences; here, Laufer had no intent to book and alleges only that the website lacked required details under the Attorney General’s regulations implementing 42 U.S.C. § 12182. Havens Realty does not control because it involved being personally lied to in a housing transaction—classic discriminatory treatment in a concrete encounter—while this case amounts to self-initiated monitoring of a website for compliance without any plan to transact. Extending standing on these facts would convert Article III courts into roving compliance tribunals for executive regulations, contrary to the separation of powers reflected in the Constitution’s case-or-controversy limit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, and under Spokeo and TransUnion a bare statutory or regulatory violation—divorced from real-world harm—is not enough. Havens Realty involved an individual plaintiff who personally received a discriminatory misrepresentation prohibited by statute, but here the alleged omission on a publicly available reservation page, viewed with no intent to book, is more like an abstract interest in compliance than a concrete injury. Title III and the DOJ reservation-rule (28 C.F.R. Part 36) aim to facilitate equal access to lodging services, and without a good-faith plan to use the information to book a room, the claimed “informational injury” lacks the practical nexus that makes it concrete and workable under Article III. Extending standing to no-intent website testers would risk transforming federal courts into general compliance monitors, contrary to judicial restraint and the limits emphasized in TransUnion.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury in fact, and “an injury in law is not an injury in fact.” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190, 2205 (2021). Laufer alleges only that the hotel’s online reservation system omitted accessibility information required by DOJ’s Title III regulations, but she had no intent to book a room and thus identifies no “downstream consequences” or real-world harm from the missing information as TransUnion and Spokeo require for informational injuries to be concrete. Havens Realty recognized tester standing where the plaintiff was personally subjected to statutorily prohibited discriminatory treatment—being lied to about housing availability—whereas this claim more closely resembles a bare regulatory noncompliance divorced from any concrete effect on the plaintiff’s conduct. Absent an intent to use the reservation system to secure lodging, the asserted harm is an abstract interest in statutory compliance, insufficient for Article III standing under TransUnion and Spokeo.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III and the Attorney General’s reservation regulations require hotels to provide accessibility information through booking channels, and denial of that information to a disabled individual is itself a concrete, discriminatory harm cognizable under Article III. As in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, a “tester” suffers injury when she is personally subjected to statutorily prohibited differential treatment—here, being denied mandated accessibility information—regardless of her intent to transact. Spokeo recognizes informational deprivation as potentially concrete, and TransUnion’s concern about “downstream consequences” is satisfied in this civil-rights context because the missing information functions as discriminatory treatment that predictably burdens equal access to the marketplace. Denying standing would undermine Congress’s and DOJ’s chosen enforcement mechanism for practical, widespread online-access barriers, contrary to the ADA’s equal-access mandate in 42 U.S.C. § 12182.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ADA “tester” who visits a hotel’s online reservation system solely to check for accessibility information—without any intent to book a room—suffers an Article III injury in fact (typically framed as an “informational injury”) sufficient for standing to sue under Title III.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing/injury in fact), and Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189, including DOJ’s implementing regulation commonly called the “Reservation Rule” (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Acheson Hotels argues Laufer lacks Article III standing because she had no plan to stay at the hotel and thus suffered no concrete, real-world harm; merely encountering missing accessibility information on a website—when sought only to generate litigation—does not constitute a concrete injury. Petitioner further contends that treating this as a cognizable “informational injury” improperly expands tester standing beyond permissible limits and conflicts with modern standing decisions (e.g., Spokeo and TransUnion) that require a concrete harm (or at least downstream consequences) rather than a bare statutory/regulatory violation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Laufer argues she has standing because Title III and the Reservation Rule entitle disabled individuals to specified accessibility information as part of equal access to hotel services, and denial of that required information is itself a concrete discriminatory harm—an informational injury—regardless of her intent to book a room. She relies on the principle recognized in Havens Realty that testers can suffer injury when they are personally denied information they are legally entitled to receive, even if they sought the information only to test compliance.
key_precedents: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190 (2021)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
United States v. Symonevich, 688 F.3d 12 (1st Cir. 2012) (implicit overruling skepticism)
In re Sealed Case, 151 F.3d 1059 (D.C. Cir. 1998) (dicta/footnote overruling skepticism)
McCoy v. Mass. Inst. of Tech., 950 F.2d 13 (1st Cir. 1991) (weight of Supreme Court dicta)
Bais Yaakov of Spring Valley v. ACT, Inc., 798 F.3d 46 (1st Cir. 2015) (prior holding vs later dicta)
United States v. Báez-Martínez, 950 F.3d 119 (1st Cir. 2020) (treatment of dicta)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Havens-based argument is the most forceful: that denial of legally required information to a tester can itself be a concrete injury. But Spokeo and TransUnion require that the asserted informational deprivation bear a close relationship to a traditionally cognizable harm or have practical consequences, and Laufer’s conceded lack of intent to book makes this omission functionally a generalized compliance grievance rather than a denial of access in any real sense. Justice Kagan’s proposed administrable limitation—requiring at least a genuine intent to use the service or comparable practical stake—best harmonizes Havens’s transactional misrepresentation context with TransUnion’s concreteness rule and allows a narrow holding on these facts without purporting to abolish tester standing categorically. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern reinforces that a regulation specifying disclosures cannot by itself manufacture Article III injury where the plaintiff alleges no downstream impediment to using the service.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Havens Realty does not overcome Article III’s demand for a concrete injury, because Havens involved a direct, individualized act of discriminatory misrepresentation in an actual housing transaction context, while this case alleges only regulatory noncompliance encountered during a self-initiated search with no intent to book. Spokeo and TransUnion, as the Chief Justice notes, reject the proposition that a statutorily (or regulatorily) created right to information “automatically” yields standing absent a harm with a close historical analogue or real-world consequences, and Laufer pleads neither. A plaintiff who never planned to use the service suffers no denial of equal access in any practical sense; she asserts an injury in law untethered to any concrete deprivation. Recognizing standing here would allow regulations and private litigants to expand federal jurisdiction beyond the Constitution’s case-or-controversy limits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Havens-based argument is the best for respondent, but Havens involved a statute that made the misrepresentation to the tester in a live housing inquiry the discriminatory act itself; here, Laufer’s conceded lack of intent to book means the alleged omission produced no practical denial of access to lodging services and reads as an abstract compliance audit. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Spokeo and especially TransUnion require a concrete injury with a close relationship to traditionally recognized harms or some real-world consequence, and the mere absence of regulatory-mandated information—encountered during a self-initiated search undertaken solely to sue—does not satisfy that standard. Justice Jackson’s point that intent-to-transact limits could reduce Title III enforcement cannot overcome Article III’s case-or-controversy requirement; Congress (and certainly an agency regulation) cannot dispense with concreteness to create federal jurisdiction. I would reverse narrowly on these facts while leaving open suits by genuine prospective users who are actually impeded in planning or booking due to missing accessibility information.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to insist, under Spokeo and TransUnion, that not every statutory or regulatory violation is concrete injury—but their “intent to book” limiter mischaracterizes the harm here as merely technical. The Reservation Rule defines what equal access to the reservation service entails; when Laufer encounters a public-facing booking interface that withholds required accessibility information, she is personally denied information she has a legal right to receive, which Havens treats as a concrete, individualized injury even for a tester. TransUnion’s concern with “bare” violations is met because the omission implicates the ADA’s core anti-exclusion interest—equal informational access in the marketplace—not a divorced procedural defect; requiring subjective intent to transact would, as Justice Jackson notes, effectively immunize online discrimination that occurs at the information-gathering stage. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers worry doesn’t move me because Congress in Title III delegated to DOJ the authority to specify how equal access is provided, and the Article III injury flows from the plaintiff’s personal denial of that access, not from the regulation “manufacturing” jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Havens-based argument is the hardest point: when a statute makes the denial of information itself the discrimination, a tester can suffer a concrete injury upon being personally refused that information. But Spokeo and especially TransUnion require that the asserted informational deprivation map onto a traditionally cognizable harm or carry some real-world consequence; on these facts, Laufer’s conceded lack of intent to book makes the omission functionally incapable of denying her equal access to the hotel’s service in any practical sense. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we can read Havens narrowly as involving an individualized misrepresentation in a transactional setting, while this case looks like a self-initiated compliance audit untethered to use, which Article III does not permit federal courts to adjudicate. Justice Jackson is right that an intent-to-transact requirement could weaken Title III enforcement in some online contexts, but a workable middle ground is to demand at least a genuine plan to use the service (or comparable downstream effect) so that the informational denial is not merely an invitation to litigate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Havens-based account remains the most serious objection, because it treats the personal denial of legally required information as a concrete injury even for a tester. But Spokeo and TransUnion require more than an “injury in law,” and on these facts Laufer’s conceded no-intent-to-book posture leaves only an abstract interest in regulatory compliance untethered to any practical denial of access or downstream consequence—unlike Havens’s transactional misrepresentation that the statute itself defined as discriminatory treatment of the individual. Justice Kagan’s limiting principle—requiring some genuine intent to use the service or a comparable practical stake—best harmonizes Havens with TransUnion while respecting separation-of-powers constraints; otherwise, as the Chief Justice suggests, an executive regulation could effectively expand Article III jurisdiction by converting any noncompliant website into a justiciable case. Title III’s authorization for DOJ rulemaking cannot eliminate the Constitution’s concreteness requirement, and I do not see a historical analogue that would treat this kind of self-initiated, no-stakes “audit” as a traditionally cognizable injury.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Havens treats a tester’s personal denial of legally required information as a concrete injury, and Justice Jackson persuasively frames the Reservation Rule as part of equal access to the reservation service. But under Spokeo and especially TransUnion, we still must ask whether the asserted informational deprivation is concrete in the sense of bearing a close historical analogue or causing a real-world effect; Laufer’s conceded lack of intent to book makes this omission functionally irrelevant to her own access and collapses into an abstract compliance grievance. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Havens involved a direct, individualized discriminatory misrepresentation in a transactional setting, whereas this case resembles a self-initiated audit of regulatory compliance untethered to any contemplated use—an administrable distinction that preserves precedent while enforcing Article III limits. DOJ’s regulatory authority under Title III cannot itself supply concreteness where the plaintiff has no practical stake, so I remain for reversal on standing on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is her reading of Havens: that a tester’s personal denial of legally required information can itself be the discriminatory harm. But Spokeo and TransUnion, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, require a concrete injury with a close relationship to a traditionally cognizable harm or a real-world consequence, and Laufer’s conceded lack of intent to book leaves the omission untethered to any practical denial of access—more like a generalized compliance audit than individualized discrimination. I agree with Justice Kagan’s proposed administrable limitation that some genuine intent to use the service (or a comparable practical stake) is necessary to keep informational-injury doctrine from collapsing Article III into regulatory noncompliance. Havens is best confined to its transactional misrepresentation setting where the statute itself made the misrepresentation unlawful treatment of the individual, and the Reservation Rule cannot, without more, supply concreteness for a plaintiff who never sought to use the lodging service.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I am not persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s proposed “intent-to-book” limiter, because it effectively converts Title III’s equal-access obligation for reservation services into a subjective-use test that is hard to administer and would, as a practical matter, shield pervasive online noncompliance from the ADA’s injunctive scheme. Spokeo and TransUnion do require more than a bare legal violation, but this is not an abstract procedural defect: under Havens Realty, the personal denial of information the law makes available to the individual can itself be a concrete, individualized injury, and the Reservation Rule makes accessibility information part of the reservation-service access that disabled users are entitled to on equal terms. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern doesn’t defeat standing here because Article III concreteness comes from the plaintiff’s direct encounter with a discriminatory informational barrier in the marketplace, not from “manufactured” jurisdiction by regulation. Requiring downstream transactional intent would undervalue the real-world way disabled travelers must gather accessibility information before planning, undermining procedural fairness and the statute’s practical operation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, and this Court has emphasized in Spokeo and TransUnion that a bare statutory or regulatory violation—divorced from real-world harm or downstream consequences—does not suffice. Whatever Havens Realty’s continuing force, it involved an individualized act of discriminatory misrepresentation in the housing context, and TransUnion cautioned against treating any statutorily created right to information as automatically conferring standing. Here, where the plaintiff visited the reservation site solely to test compliance and lacked any intent to book a room, the asserted “informational injury” is too abstract to satisfy Article III absent some concrete effect or discriminatory denial of service. A narrow disposition denying standing on these facts best respects precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy without rewriting Title III or the Reservation Rule, 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III demands a concrete injury in fact, not merely an injury in law created by statute or regulation, and a plaintiff who never intended to book a room alleges only a bare noncompliance with the ADA’s Reservation Rule rather than any real-world harm. Under Spokeo and TransUnion, a statutory or regulatory violation does not “automatically” confer standing absent a historically rooted or otherwise concrete harm, and Laufer’s self-inflicted search for missing website information—without any plan to use the service—fails that requirement. Havens Realty does not compel a contrary result here because it involved a direct, individualized act of discriminatory misrepresentation in housing, whereas this case alleges only an abstract deprivation of information untethered to any intended transaction or downstream consequences. To preserve the Constitution’s limits on the federal judicial power, I would hold Laufer lacks standing and reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, not merely a regulatory violation untethered to any real-world effect, and Laufer’s admitted lack of any intent to book a room makes the missing accessibility information incapable of causing her a concrete harm. Under Spokeo and TransUnion, a plaintiff cannot manufacture standing by pointing to a bare statutory or regulatory right to information where the deprivation has no downstream consequences and resembles no traditionally cognizable injury. Havens Realty is best read as limited to the FHA’s specific prohibition on misrepresentation to an individual who was personally subjected to discriminatory treatment in the transaction context; it does not license internet-wide “tester” suits where the plaintiff sought information solely to sue and never intended to use the service governed by Title III and 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e). Extending standing here would invite massive private enforcement divorced from actual discrimination-in-fact, with serious practical consequences inconsistent with Article III’s separation-of-powers limits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III and DOJ’s Reservation Rule, 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e), create a legally protected right for disabled individuals to receive accessibility information necessary for equal access to hotel reservation services, and Laufer alleges she personally encountered its denial on the hotel’s reservation system. Under Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, a tester suffers an Article III injury when she is personally denied information she has a statutory right to receive, even if she sought it only to test compliance. Spokeo and TransUnion require concreteness, but they do not erase Havens where the denial itself is the discriminatory harm—here, exclusion from equal informational access in a marketplace service—rather than a technical violation divorced from any protected interest. Denying standing would substantially weaken Title III’s practical enforceability and leave systemic, low-visibility barriers unremedied, undermining Congress’s remedial scheme for vulnerable populations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, and under Spokeo and TransUnion a plaintiff generally cannot rest standing on a bare statutory or regulatory violation divorced from real-world harm. The Reservation Rule, 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e), is designed to facilitate equal access to hotel reservations, but a plaintiff who concedes she had no intent to book a room is not plausibly harmed in the way the rule targets—her alleged injury is informational only in an abstract sense. Havens Realty is best read as recognizing tester standing when a plaintiff is personally subjected to the kind of discriminatory misrepresentation the statute directly forbids in a transactional setting; extending it to website “testers” with no plan to transact would expand informational-injury standing beyond the limits emphasized in TransUnion. A workable, coherent rule is that Title III plaintiffs must at least show a genuine intent to use the service (or some comparable downstream consequence) so the missing information causes a concrete impediment rather than merely supporting litigation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete, real-world injury, not just a regulatory violation untethered to any practical effect. Under Spokeo and TransUnion, an asserted “informational injury” is cognizable only when the plaintiff is denied information in a way that bears a close relationship to a traditionally recognized harm or has downstream consequences; a self-appointed tester who never intended to book a room alleges neither. Havens Realty is best read as turning on a statute that made the denial of truthful housing-availability information itself the discrimination and thus the concrete injury, whereas Title III’s Reservation Rule (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)) cannot by regulation alone manufacture Article III injury for a plaintiff with no intent to use the service. Allowing standing here would relax separation-of-powers limits by permitting the Executive (through regulation) and private litigants to expand federal jurisdiction beyond Article III’s case-or-controversy requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury, not a bare regulatory violation divorced from any real-world effect. Under Spokeo and especially TransUnion, an asserted “informational injury” is cognizable only when the plaintiff is denied information in a way that causes, or at least closely resembles, a traditionally recognized harm; here, Laufer had no intent to book a room, so the missing reservation information did not affect her access to the hotel’s services in any practical sense. Havens Realty is distinguishable because the tester there was personally subjected to a denial that directly implicated the statutory right in a concrete transactional setting; extending Havens to no-intent, website-only “testers” would expand standing in a way that is difficult to cabin and invites unworkable mass litigation under Title III (42 U.S.C. § 12188(a)(1)) and the Reservation Rule (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)). Judicial restraint and the need for administrable standing rules counsel requiring a good-faith intent to use the service when the alleged injury is missing public-facing information.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a concrete injury in fact, and under Spokeo and TransUnion a bare violation of a statutory or regulatory requirement—divorced from real-world harm or a close common-law analogue—does not suffice. Title III’s Reservation Rule, 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e), regulates the content of accessibility information in reservation systems, but Laufer’s admitted lack of any intent to book means the alleged omission did not impair her ability to obtain the hotel’s services and thus resembles an abstract compliance grievance. Havens Realty is best read as involving a denial of truthful information that functioned as a classic discriminatory misrepresentation with a historically recognized harm, whereas here the claimed “informational injury” is untethered to any prospective transaction or downstream consequences. Methodologically, recognizing standing on these facts would expand informational-injury standing beyond the limits Spokeo and TransUnion reaffirmed, effectively permitting suits based solely on regulatory noncompliance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III and DOJ’s Reservation Rule, 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e), create a concrete entitlement for disabled individuals to receive specific accessibility information as part of equal access to a hotel’s reservation service; denial of that information to the individual who requested it is a particularized injury, even if she sought it as a tester. Under Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, a tester suffers Article III injury when she is personally denied information she is legally entitled to receive, and that principle can coexist with Spokeo and TransUnion because the harm is not a “bare” procedural violation but the real-world deprivation of mandated information in the marketplace. TransUnion’s demand for concreteness is satisfied where the plaintiff alleges the defendant failed to provide required information to her in the ordinary course of offering services, producing the precise exclusionary effect the ADA targets (even if the remedy is injunctive under 42 U.S.C. § 12188(a)(1)). As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences, foreclosing standing here would substantially undercut Title III’s enforcement mechanism for widespread online noncompliance that burdens people with disabilities.
